title: Piano Concerto No. 2 in G major
hook: The concerto Tchaikovsky liked “far more than the first”, heard here as he wrote it, solo violin and cello included.

painting.title: Young Man Playing the Piano
painting.pairingNote: A young Parisian alone at his grand piano, painted three years before Tchaikovsky wrote this concerto’s finale in Paris; the piano on its own, as it so often is in this concerto.

facts: Tchaikovsky began the concerto in October 1879 at his sister’s estate at Kamenka, in Ukraine, wrote the finale in Paris that November and orchestrated it at Kamenka in the spring of 1880. He scored it without trombones or tuba.

He dedicated it to Nikolai Rubinstein, who had once savaged his First Concerto and then become its champion. Rubinstein died in March 1881 before he could play it, and the first performance took place in New York on 12 November 1881, with the pianist Madeline Schiller and the conductor Theodore Thomas.

Tchaikovsky was disappointed that the concerto never caught on, and late in life wrote that he liked it “far more than the first”. His pupil Alexander Siloti pressed him for cuts; Tchaikovsky refused most of them. Siloti’s edition, published in 1897 after the composer’s death, cut and rearranged the first two movements, removed most of the solo violin and cello in the slow movement, and was for decades the version everyone played. Tchaikovsky’s original was published in 1955.

The concerto is unusual in how often piano and orchestra take turns rather than playing together. Its first movement has a long solo [[cadenza|cadenza]], and its slow movement turns for long stretches into chamber music for piano, violin and cello.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a proud, festive march with a huge solo cadenza (I), a tender song for a [[piano-trio|piano trio]] inside the orchestra (II), a quick, carnival-like dance (III).

movements.heading: Allegro brillante
movements.summary: The orchestra opens with a proud, march-like theme, and the piano takes it up at once. The movement is in [[sonata-form|sonata form]], but built in large blocks: the orchestra plays, then the piano plays, and they rarely mix. Its centre is a solo cadenza several minutes long, the climax of the movement, placed in the middle rather than near the end.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 1, the march
mainIdeas.description: bold and festive, stepping up and down from the home note, with a crisp rhythm.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 2
mainIdeas.description: tender and singing, in E-flat major, first on clarinet and horn over quivering strings.

stops.hear: The full orchestra plays a proud, festive march tune
The piano takes up the march in big, ringing chords
Piano and orchestra take turns; the piano often plays alone in brilliant, free passages
Quiet and tender: clarinet and horn sing a new tune over quivering strings
stops.happening: Theme 2, in E-flat major, with string [[tremolo|tremolo]]

stops.hear: The piano takes over the tender tune and decorates it
The orchestra alone, loud, back to the march
The themes move through new keys; orchestra and piano still alternate
The orchestra stops; the piano alone, building from murmurs to thunderous octaves
stops.happening: The great cadenza, the development’s second part

stops.hear: The march tune returns in the orchestra
The tender tune again, now in the home key

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: Faster and louder, piano and orchestra together at last

notice: Count how often you hear the piano alone and the orchestra alone. Tchaikovsky once said he could not stand the sound of piano and orchestra together; here he mostly keeps them apart.
In the cadenza the piano builds the movement’s climax entirely on its own. Notice how long the orchestra stays silent.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Nebolsin plays Tchaikovsky’s original version, without Siloti’s cuts. The concerto was recorded in Wellington in November 2014 with the New Zealand Symphony Orchestra.

movements.heading: Andante non troppo
movements.summary: A slow movement in D major in which the piano is, for long stretches, only one of three soloists. A solo violin sings the long main melody, a solo cello takes it up, and the piano joins them so that the three play almost like a [[piano-trio|piano trio]] with the orchestra around them. In the middle the music speeds up and the piano has a cadenza of its own; then the melody returns, shared by all three.

mainIdeas.name: The main melody
mainIdeas.description: long, warm and nostalgic, first on the solo violin.

mainIdeas.name: The trio
mainIdeas.description: piano, violin and cello in close conversation.

stops.hear: Soft strings, then a solo violin sings a long, warm melody
stops.happening: The main theme, on the violin

stops.hear: A solo cello takes up the melody; the violin weaves around it
The piano enters quietly and sings the melody in its own way
Piano, violin and cello play together, passing phrases between them, with the orchestra softly behind
The music grows faster and more urgent
The orchestra and the other soloists stop; the piano alone
The main melody returns, violin and cello singing it together
stops.happening: The return of the theme, as a duet

stops.label: Last 2 minutes
stops.hear: All three soloists and the orchestra close very quietly in D major

notice: Listen for how long the piano waits before it enters. For the first minutes this is a violin and cello concerto.
This is the music Siloti cut most heavily. Most of the violin and cello solos you hear were missing from performances for decades.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: The violin and cello soloists are the orchestra’s own players: the concertmaster Vesa-Matti Leppänen and the cellist Andrew Joyce.

movements.heading: Allegro con fuoco
movements.summary: A short, quick finale in a skipping, dotted two-beat rhythm. Three lively, carnival-like tunes follow one another in a loose [[rondo|rondo]], and here, for once, piano and orchestra play closely together. There is no cadenza; the end is a blaze of piano and orchestra that recalls the close of the First Concerto.

mainIdeas.name: Tune 1
mainIdeas.description: quick and skipping, in a dotted rhythm.

mainIdeas.name: Tune 3
mainIdeas.description: another contrasting idea, with the piano sparkling in its high register.

stops.hear: A quick, skipping tune in a dotted rhythm, tossed between piano and orchestra
stops.happening: The first tune, in G major

stops.hear: A second tune with a more exotic colour
Another new tune, the piano sparkling high above the orchestra
The skipping tune returns
The tunes return in new keys; piano and orchestra play closely together
The skipping tune once more, in the home key
Faster and louder, building to the end

stops.label: Last 20 seconds
stops.hear: Blazing flourishes from piano and orchestra, and the final chords in G major

notice: Notice how short this movement is after the first two. It lasts about a third as long as the first movement.
Listen to the very end: its blazing close for piano and full orchestra looks back to the end of the First Concerto.

threads.title: Piano alone, orchestra alone
threads.body: In the first two movements piano and orchestra mostly take turns. Only in the finale do they play as one.

threads.title: A concerto with three soloists
threads.body: The slow movement’s violin and cello make the piece, for a while, almost a triple concerto. Tchaikovsky’s former pupil Sergei Taneyev, who gave the first Russian performance, criticised exactly that.

threads.title: Siloti’s version
threads.body: For most of the 20th century the concerto was heard in Siloti’s cut edition; George Balanchine’s ballet *Ballet Imperial* (1941) used it too. Recordings of the original, like this one, have restored the work Tchaikovsky wrote.
